papers.title_en: The next frontier of athletic intelligence in sports medicine and exercise science
papers.tldr_en: This commentary argues that the next frontier of athletic intelligence will be defined not by technological sophistication alone, but by the wisdom, inclusivity and ethical resolve with which the sports medicine community deploys it.
papers.abstract_en: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming sports medicine and exercise science, offering unprecedented capabilities in markerless motion capture, automated exercise prescription, diagnostic imaging and integrated athlete monitoring. These advances have the potential to democratise biomechanical analysis, scale clinical expertise to underserved populations and shift injury management from reactive treatment to predictive prevention. However, the pace of adoption carries significant risks, including technological dependency without methodological literacy, the entrenchment of global inequities through biased training datasets and models, the erosion of clinician-athlete relationships and a widening governance vacuum over data ownership and algorithmic accountability. papers.journal: BMC Sports Science Medicine and Rehabilitation
papers.journal_tier: 康复医学2区/运动科学3区
papers.tldr_en: Evaluating the clinical efficacy of wearable sensor–based gait analysis for injury prevention in athletes, examining its role in rehabilitation monitoring and clinical decision-making, and identifying methodological limitations and future research priorities required for standardized clinical integration identifies key challenges.
papers.abstract_en: Gait analysis is fundamental for optimizing athletic performance and mitigating injury risks in sports medicine. While traditional laboratory assessments offer insights, the emergence of wearable sensor technology provides novel opportunities for objective, real-time gait evaluation in ecologically valid settings. This systematic review aims to (1) evaluate the clinical efficacy of wearable sensor–based gait analysis for injury prevention in athletes (2), examine its role in rehabilitation monitoring and clinical decision-making, and (3) identify methodological limitations and future research priorities required for standardized clinical integration. Adhering to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic search was conducted across MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase from inception to May 31st, 2025. papers.title_en: Building for the Future: A Systematic Review of the Effects of Eccentric Resistance Training on Measures of Physical Performance in Youth Athletes
papers.tldr_en: The findings of this systematic review support the inclusion of eccentric resistance training in youth athletes to improve measures of muscular strength, jump, sprint and change of direction performance.
papers.abstract_en: Background Eccentric resistance training is recognised as an effective stimulus for enhancing measures of muscular strength and power in adult populations; however, its value in youth athletes is currently not well understood. Objective The aim of this systematic review was to critically appraise the effects of eccentric resistance training on measures of physical performance (i.e. muscular strength, jump, sprint and change of direction) in youth athletes 18 years of age and under. Methods Original journal articles published between 1950 and June 2022 were retrieved from electronic search engines of PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Google Scholar’s advanced search option. papers.title_en: Effects of different dietary supplements combined with conditioning training on muscle strength, jump performance, sprint speed, and muscle mass in athletes: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
papers.tldr_en: Protein supplementation appears to be the most effective strategy for increasing muscular strength; β-alanine and creatine both improve jump performance, with β-alanine offering marginally superior effectiveness; and creatine is particularly beneficial for sprint speed.
papers.abstract_en: Background As dietary supplements have become integral to meeting athletes’ specialised nutritional requirements, research into their effects on performance has intensified. Yet inconsistent findings leave the efficacy of some supplements—most notably branched-chain amino acids and β-hydroxy-β-methylbutyrate (HMB)—open to debate. To clarify which products offer the greatest benefit, we undertook a systematic review and network meta-analysis aimed at identifying the supplements most effective for athletes, including protein, creatine, β-alanine, HMB, vitamin D, caffeine, and others. Methods PubMed, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, Embase and SPORTDiscus were searched from database inception to 15 March 2024 for RCTs evaluating the effects of dietary supplements (including but not limited to protein, creatine, β-alanine, HMB, caffeine, and vitamin D) on athletic performance. papers.title_en: Reducing the Risk of Unintentional Doping From Supplements: A Practical Guide for Athletes and Support Teams
papers.tldr_en: The proposed framework integrates efficacy, evidence quality, mechanisms of action, contamination pathways, behavioural determinants, strict liability and antidoping risk to support safer supplementation decisions to protect athlete health and the integrity of clean sport.
papers.abstract_en: Context Dietary supplements are widely used across all levels of sport. While the ‘food first but not food only’ approach remains central to sports nutrition, selected supplements may support performance, recovery or health when used appropriately. However, variable regulation, product contamination, mislabelling and inappropriate decision‐making may expose athletes to inadvertent antidoping rule violations (ADRVs). Evidence Acquisition This structured narrative review searched PubMed and Scopus for literature published between January 2000 and December 2025. Evidence from primary studies, randomised controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta‐analyses, mechanistic studies, contamination analyses, behavioural research, consensus statements and official guidance documents from major sports and antidoping organisations was critically evaluated and synthesised. papers.title_en: The impact of microdosed plyometric training on speed and explosive abilities of football players during the pre-season
papers.journal: BMC Sports Science Medicine and Rehabilitation
papers.journal_tier: 康复医学2区/运动科学3区
papers.abstract_en: Background Microdosed training distributes a given training stimulus into shorter, more frequent sessions. This study investigated whether a microdosed plyometric program produces similar adaptations to a traditional plyometric program when the total number of plyometric contacts is closely matched in elite youth football players. Allocation was nonrandomized and matched on countermovement jump (CMJ) height and modified reactive strength index (RSI mod) from a drop jump (DJ), with standing broad jump (SBJ) used as a tiebreaker.
